summary: Specifies a ROHC profile for compressing TCP/IP headers, including common options such as SACK and Timestamps. It works well over links with significant error rates and long round-trip times. It was replaced by RFC 6846.

eli5.summary: A way to shrink the labels on TCP packets, even over a bumpy link. A newer RFC replaced this.

questions: how does rohc handle packet loss
how small can tcp headers get
subtitle: Robust compression of TCP/IP headers for links with errors and delays.

tldr.problem: TCP/IP headers are large relative to payload on bandwidth-limited and error-prone links (satellite, wireless), and existing compression schemes (CTCP, IPHC) fail when packets are lost or cannot handle TCP options like SACK and Timestamps effectively.
tldr.mechanism: ROHC-TCP provides a framework using a compressor and decompressor with explicit feedback channels. It uses three packet types (IR, IR-DYN, CO) and maintains compression state across packets, leveraging list compression for TCP options and detecting field change patterns to minimize transmitted header information.
tldr.outcome: TCP/IP headers can be shrunk to 6-8 bytes on stable flows and even 8-15 bytes on acknowledgments with options, while remaining robust on lossy links. RFC 6846 later superseded this specification.

today: RFC 4996 defined ROHC-TCP compression and is an Internet Standard, but it was superseded by RFC 6846, which provides updated procedures. New implementations should refer to RFC 6846 for current requirements.

sections.title: The Problem with Existing Compression
sections.content:
On low-speed or medium-speed links, TCP/IP headers consume significant bandwidth. A typical TCP/IP header is 40 to 60 bytes, while the payload might be only a few bytes (for acknowledgments). Header compression is valuable to reclaim bandwidth, but prior schemes had fatal limitations on lossy links.

CTCP (Compressed TCP, RFC 1144) detects retransmissions and sends full context updates, but a single packet loss desynchronizes the compressor and decompressor, causing all subsequent packets to fail checksums until a timeout forces a retransmission.

IPHC (IP Header Compression, RFC 2507) improves CTCP with local repair and feedback-based recovery, but still struggles with TCP options. Any change in the options field (such as a Timestamp change or new SACK option) makes the entire field uncompressible, and handshake packets (SYN, FIN) cannot be compressed at all.
sections.eli5: Old compression breaks when packets get lost on a bad link. ROHC fixes that by recovering from losses and handling more types of packets.

sections.title: ROHC Framework and TCP Profile
sections.content:
The ROHC (Robust Header Compression) framework, defined in RFC 3095, allows different profiles to be defined for different protocol sets or compression strategies. RFC 4996 defines a specific profile for TCP/IP compression, identified by profile number 0x0006.

ROHC-TCP overcomes the limitations of earlier schemes by being robust against packet loss, efficiently compressing TCP options including SACK and Timestamps, and compressing handshake packets (SYN, FIN). The approach is fundamentally different: instead of trying to infer all field values from a reference packet (as CTCP and IPHC do), ROHC-TCP sends explicit context updates using multiple packet types, allowing graceful recovery from losses.
sections.eli5: ROHC is a flexible framework for compression. The TCP version fixes the old problems by sending updates more explicitly so the receiver can stay in sync even on a lossy link.

sections.title: Compressor and Decompressor Interaction
sections.content:
ROHC-TCP operates as a state machine where the compressor must always know the decompressor's state of knowledge. The compressor uses an optimistic approach: it sends the same information for multiple packets until it gains confidence that the decompressor has received it. Without feedback, the compressor periodically refreshes context by sending larger packets that carry more information.

The decompressor operates in three states: No Context (NC), where it cannot decompress anything; Static Context (SC), where it has the static fields but not dynamic ones; and Full Context (FC), where both are valid. It moves downward (to lower states) only when CRC checks fail repeatedly, indicating context damage. When the decompressor successfully verifies a packet using CRC, it updates its context with the new information.
sections.eli5: The sender keeps sending the same info until sure the receiver got it. The receiver tracks what it knows and asks for a refresh if something seems wrong. Both check their work with CRC.

sections.title: Packet Types and Context Initialization
sections.content:
ROHC-TCP defines three primary packet types. IR (Initialization and Refresh) packets carry full static and dynamic information with an 8-bit CRC; they are used to initialize a context and to periodically refresh both static and dynamic state. IR-DYN (IR Dynamic) packets refresh only the dynamic part with an 8-bit CRC, useful when static fields have not changed.

For steady-state compression, CO (Compressed) packets send only the changed fields with a 3-bit or 7-bit CRC. The smaller CRC is used when the compressor is confident the decompressor will need less detailed information.

For multiple short-lived flows (like web browsing with many small connections), IR-CR (Context Replication) packets copy an existing validated context to a new flow, avoiding the full IR overhead and accelerating context establishment.

The compressor includes a Master Sequence Number (MSN) field—a counter incremented for each packet—that allows the decompressor to track which packet the compressor is sending and helps recover from errors through feedback.
sections.eli5: The sender has four types of packets: Full update (IR), just-dynamics update (IR-DYN), tiny update (CO), and fast-copy for new flows (IR-CR). Each uses a number to say which packet it is.

sections.title: Compressing TCP Options
sections.content:
TCP options—such as Maximum Segment Size (MSS), Window Scale (WSCALE), SACK (Selective Acknowledgments), and Timestamps—are common in modern TCP but pose compression challenges because they change unpredictably.

ROHC-TCP handles TCP options using list compression. The compressor maintains an item table mapping frequently used options to indexes. On context initialization, the full list of options is transmitted. In subsequent packets, only the presence of options and any changed content are sent. When the option list structure changes (new options appear or old ones disappear), a compressed representation of the new list is sent.

This approach is far more efficient than prior schemes where any option change made the entire options field uncompressible.
sections.eli5: Options like Timestamps change a lot, but ROHC has a trick: it keeps a table of options and just says which are present and what changed, instead of sending the whole thing.

sections.title: Status and Performance
sections.content:
ROHC-TCP achieves significant compression ratios in typical scenarios. Compressed data packet headers can be as small as 6-8 bytes (compared to 52 bytes uncompressed for IPv4+TCP+Timestamps), and ACK-only packets can be compressed to 5 bytes. These gains come with robustness on lossy links that would break earlier compression schemes.

RFC 4996 is an Internet Standard, but it was superseded by RFC 6846, which provides updated procedures and simplified rules. New implementations should refer to RFC 6846 for current requirements.
sections.eli5: ROHC-TCP can shrink headers from 52 bytes to just 5-8 bytes, and it doesn't break on a lossy link. A newer RFC replaced this one with improvements.
